transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-14
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~50 minutes
Attendees: Evan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Rosa (CieloTech Head of ML), Tom (CieloTech Platform Eng), Jared (CTO)

Summary: quick run through bench snapshots, catalog tradeoffs (quantized vs float), pin matrix and soft-fallback rules, and next steps for a tabletop rollback drill.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, uh thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call?
[00:10] Rosa: Rosa here. Hey.
[00:12] Tom: Tom, on the platform side.
[00:14] Jared: Jared, CTO.
[00:16] Priya: Priya from Redwood, hi.
[00:18] Evan: Cool, alright we're about 50 minutes, goal is to be practical: pick a small catalog of model variants to pin for the pilot and agree on fallback/rollback criteria, plus benches. Sound good?
[00:30] Rosa: Yup, that's the ask. We're trying to avoid surprises in production — can't have cost spike or latency regressions that break endpoints.
[00:36] Priya: Great. I shared a small spreadsheet in the chat — quick snapshot of three families we tested: rdx-7b-q4 (quant), rdx-13b-pt (int8-like), and open-llama-30b-fp16. Notes in the sheet show cost per 1k tokens and p95 latency for the current prompt set.
[01:05] Tom: We looked at that — the quantized 7b is appealing costwise but we saw hallucination uptick on long-form summarization. Is that consistent?
[01:15] Priya: yeah, it's typical — Q4 quant can increase off-by-one errors and some tokenization quirks. Our evals show a small but measurable regression on long-context QA.
[01:30] Rosa: So we care about both latency and quality; our SLA for API calls is 500ms p95 for short prompts, and 1.8s for longer ones.
[01:42] Evan: Right, and the pilot success metric Rosa outlined last week was: <=2% quality regression vs baseline on the eval set, and p95 under SLA.
[01:52] Jared: Also want an escape hatch that won't require full code rollbacks — some routing rule or quick pin switch.
[02:00] Priya: Exactly — that's where model pinning and soft fallbacks come in. Our proposal: pick two primary pins — a production pin and a warm-standby pin. Production pin handles 100% of traffic, warm-standby is pre-warmed for quick cutover. And a cold fallback to an L2 cheaper model if capacity or cost spikes.
[02:25] Rosa: Walk through a concrete example?
[02:28] Priya: Sure. Example: prod pin = rdx-13b-pt (best quality), warm-standby = rdx-7b-q4 (fast + cheap but slightly lower quality), cold fallback = open-llama-30b-fp16 or even a distilled 6b if needed. Policies: if regression metric >2% OR p95 > SLA for two consecutive 10-minute windows, auto-route 30% to warm-standby and alert; if still failing after 20 minutes, fail open to cold fallback and create incident.
[03:00] Tom: How automatic is that? Can we control thresholds? We need RBAC and an override so platform team can hold a manual cut.
[03:10] Priya: All configurable. We surface thresholds in the Console; you can make them soft (recommendation) or hard (enforced). RBAC integrates with SAML/SSO so only ops can flip overrides.
[03:22] Jared: Good. On the bench numbers — I saw p95 for rdx-13b-pt at 1.2s which is acceptable, cost is higher though. Any knob on batching or caching to reduce cost?
[03:34] Priya: Yes. Two levers: smarter prefix KV caching for repeated prompts and dynamic batching (sequence-length aware). For your workload distribution that Tom provided (mostly short prompts, 60% are under 50 tokens), batching helps a lot on throughput and cost per token without blowing p95. We can propose initial batch size targets.
[03:56] Rosa: About catalog differences: are quantized models always going to be unstable on our longer prompts? Or is that an artifact of the particular family?
[04:06] Priya: It varies. For some architectures, quantization is very tight and works well. For others, especially ones with certain tokenizers, you see degens. We flagged examples in the sheet. We also recommend running 3 bench rounds with your canonical prompts to see real behavior.
[04:26] Evan: Quick question for Tom — what's your comfort level giving staging VPC access for Redwood to run the benches in your network? We can also run against your staging endpoints with synthetic load if you prefer.
[04:38] Tom: We can provide a role-limited IAM and a temporary VPC peering — security team ok with that as long as logs are routed to our SIEM. We'll drop details in the ticket.
[04:48] Evan: Great, add a note — Redwood will respect retention and KMS rules. We'll include that in the security doc.
[04:54] Rosa: Competitors — we also looked at Anthropic's endpoint for a bench. Anthropic had slightly different latency profile but cost was higher; we flagged it as a possible backup if model quality trumps cost.
[05:10] Priya: Noted. On rollback playbooks: we propose a tabletop with three scenarios: sudden latency spike, quality regression, and capacity exhaustion. Each scenario will run through detection thresholds, routing steps, communication notes, and incident roles (owner, comms, oncall).
[05:34] Jared: How long to switch pins? If we need to flip to warm-standby, is it seconds, or minutes?
[05:40] Priya: If warm-standby is pre-warmed and KV cache is shared, route change is essentially immediate — sub-second for routing flag change, but warm-standby microcold misses might add tail latency. Cold fallback (spinning new instances) can be a few minutes unless pre-provisioned.
[05:58] Tom: Are there constraints on the model variants you can route between? For instance, can you route rdx-13b and an open-llama variant seamlessly?
[06:06] Priya: Yes, as long as they are API-compatible in input/output schema. We do some normalization for tokenization differences and give you a compatibility matrix. There are edge cases — e.g., different EOS tokens or structured output variations — we call those out.
[06:24] Rosa: Let's talk concrete pin list to start: I want a conservative approach. Option A: pin rdx-13b-pt prod; rdx-7b-q4 warm-standby; open-llama-30b-fp16 cold fallback. Option B: prod = rdx-13b-pt, warm-standby = rdx-13b-q4 (same family but quantized), cold fallback = distilled-6b. Thoughts?
[06:50] Priya: Option B reduces normalization issues because warm-standby is same family — less chance of behavioral deltas. But cost savings smaller. Option A gives cost win with more risk on behavioral change.
[07:03] Evan: From a rollout safety perspective I usually recommend same-family warm-standby for first two weeks to observe behavior, then you can trial cross-family cheap fallbacks. That reduces surprise regressions.
[07:14] Rosa: Ok let's do that — start with Option B for first 2 weeks. We'll agree to a cross-family emergency cold fallback only.
[07:21] Tom: Sounds good. What's the gating for moving to Option A later?
[07:25] Priya: Pass three bench runs with QA <1% regression, p95 under SLA for 24 hours of traffic replay, and a tabletop done. Then Canary 10% traffic to Option A for 2 days with monitoring.
[07:40] Rosa: Good, write that into the pin matrix.
[07:44] Evan: We'll put these thresholds in the sheet and push it to you after the call.
[07:49] Jared: A note on telemetry — we need token-level cost, p95 by route, and also a quality metric (we can use ROUGE for summarization and an entailment model for factuality). Can Redwood surface those in the console?
[08:03] Priya: Yes, we can instrument token-level cost and p95 per route, and add a custom quality metric feed if you run the eval harness. We'll show an example dashboard in the next meeting.
[08:14] Rosa: One more question — how do we handle schema changes when switching models (structured output)? We rely on JSON schema sometimes.
[08:23] Priya: We recommend function/tool-calling layer or schema validation at the proxy; Redwood can fail fast on schema mismatch and route to warm-standby or return a validation error. We'll add schema checks to the playbook.
[08:37] Evan: Alright let's recap concrete next steps.
[08:40] Priya: I will run three bench rounds using the staging access Tom provides: short (avg 30 tokens), medium (avg 200 tokens), long (avg 1k tokens). Post results and flagged examples.
[08:55] Evan: I'll put together pricing options including a reserved burst capacity note and a quick ROI calc for the two pin strategies.
[09:02] Tom: I'll open the ticket with staging VPC role and sample prompt dump.
[09:07] Rosa: I'll finalize the eval prompt set and metrics.
[09:11] Jared: Schedule tabletop for week of 2026-04-27 — I'll join.
[09:16] Evan: Excellent. Anything else?
[09:19] Rosa: Not from me.
[09:20] Tom: No.
[09:21] Priya: One small ask — in the bench results we'll include examples of degradation (inputs + outputs) so you can judge qualitatively.
[09:29] Rosa: Please do. That really helps.
[09:32] Evan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the sheet and security doc.
[09:36] End of call.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription had occasional mislabels, some technical terms spelled out (K V cache, V P C), and proper nouns normalized inconsistently.
